intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that nephrotic syndrome type 23 (NPHS23) is caused by homozygous mutation in the KIRREL1 gene (607428) on chromosome 1q23.

checks.claim: Nephrotic syndrome type 23 (NPHS23) is caused by homozygous mutation in the KIRREL1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Herein, we describe two unrelated families with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome with homozygous mutations in the KIRREL1 gene.
checks.explanation: The paper reports homozygous KIRREL1 mutations causing SRNS. The NPHS23 designation is OMIM nomenclature.

checks.claim: The KIRREL1 gene is located on chromosome 1q23.
checks.evidence_quote: Within the maximum NPL peak on chromosome 1 (arrowhead), we identified a homozygous mutation in KIRREL1 (p.Ser573Leu).
checks.explanation: The paper places KIRREL1 on chromosome 1. The 1q23 band is standard gene-location nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: Nephrotic syndrome type 23 (NPHS23) is an autosomal recessive kidney disorder. It presents with proteinuria and steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome. Some patients progress to end-stage renal disease. Renal biopsy may show focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) or other glomerular changes. KIRREL1 (NEPH1) is a component of the podocyte slit diaphragm.

checks.claim: Nephrotic syndrome type 23 (NPHS23) is an autosomal recessive kidney disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: we have identified and characterized two novel recessive mutations in KIRREL1 gene in two patients with SRNS of 2 unrelated consanguineous families
checks.explanation: The paper describes the mutations as recessive, found in the homozygous state in consanguineous families.

checks.claim: NPHS23 presents with proteinuria.
checks.evidence_quote: He has never achieved a complete remission and remained having undulating proteinuria with partial response to treatment.
checks.explanation: The patients had proteinuria.

checks.claim: NPHS23 presents with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: Both patients with detected homozygous mutations in KIRREL1 shared the phenotype of SRNS.
checks.explanation: Both patients had SRNS.

checks.claim: Some patients with NPHS23 progress to end-stage renal disease.
checks.explanation: Neither KIRREL1 patient reached end-stage renal disease. One kept normal renal function and the other reached CKD stage 2. The paper says SRNS in general progresses to ESRD, and some relatives of A666 had ESRD, but their genotypes are unknown.

checks.claim: Renal biopsy in NPHS23 may show focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) or other glomerular changes.
checks.evidence_quote: Renal histology of individual B742_21 with KIRREL1 mutation shows focal segmental glomerular sclerosis (arrows) on light microscopy (MPAS staining).
checks.explanation: One patient had FSGS. The other had mesangial hypercellularity consistent with minimal change disease, which covers 'other glomerular changes'.

checks.claim: KIRREL1 (NEPH1) is a component of the podocyte slit diaphragm.
checks.evidence_quote: we localize the expression of Neph1 to the glomerular slit diaphragm by immunogold electron microscopy in rodents
checks.explanation: Neph1 is localized to the glomerular slit diaphragm, which is formed between podocyte foot processes.

paragraphs.text: Solanki et al. (2019) reported patients from several unrelated families who had steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) beginning in childhood. Renal biopsies showed glomerular lesions, including FSGS.

checks.claim: Solanki et al. (2019) reported patients with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) from several unrelated families.
checks.evidence_quote: We discovered two homozygous missense mutations (p.Arg440Cys and p.Ser573Leu) of the KIRREL1 gene in two individuals of unrelated consanguineous families (A666 and B742) with SRNS.
checks.explanation: The paper reports two patients from two unrelated families, not patients from 'several' families.

checks.claim: The SRNS in the patients reported by Solanki et al. (2019) began in childhood.
checks.evidence_quote: The patient A666_21 was diagnosed with NS at age of 5 years.
checks.explanation: Onset was at 5 years in one patient and 14 years in the other, both in childhood ('both affected children').

checks.claim: Renal biopsies in the patients reported by Solanki et al. (2019) showed glomerular lesions, including FSGS.
checks.evidence_quote: Renal histology of individual B742_21 with KIRREL1 mutation shows focal segmental glomerular sclerosis (arrows) on light microscopy (MPAS staining).
checks.explanation: Biopsies showed glomerular lesions: FSGS in one patient and mesangial hypercellularity in both.

paragraphs.text: The transmission pattern of NPHS23 in the families reported by Solanki et al. (2019) was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

checks.claim: The transmission pattern of NPHS23 in the families reported by Solanki et al. (2019) was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.
checks.evidence_quote: we have identified and characterized two novel recessive mutations in KIRREL1 gene in two patients with SRNS of 2 unrelated consanguineous families
checks.explanation: Homozygous recessive mutations in consanguineous families fit autosomal recessive inheritance.

paragraphs.text: Solanki et al. (2019) found homozygous missense mutations in the KIRREL1 gene in patients with SRNS from unrelated families. In functional studies, the mutant KIRREL1 proteins localized abnormally and were not delivered properly to the podocyte cell membrane. The mutations also impaired the protein's interaction with other slit diaphragm components, such as nephrin.

checks.claim: Solanki et al. (2019) found homozygous missense mutations in the KIRREL1 gene in patients with SRNS from unrelated families.
checks.evidence_quote: We discovered two homozygous missense mutations (p.Arg440Cys and p.Ser573Leu) of the KIRREL1 gene in two individuals of unrelated consanguineous families (A666 and B742) with SRNS.
checks.explanation: Stated directly in the paper.

checks.claim: In functional studies by Solanki et al. (2019), the mutant KIRREL1 proteins localized abnormally.
checks.evidence_quote: In comparison to the KIRREL1 wild type, a mislocalization of both KIRREL1 mutants (Arg440Cys and Ser573Leu) was noted (Fig.2C).
checks.explanation: Stated directly in the paper.

checks.claim: In functional studies by Solanki et al. (2019), the mutant KIRREL1 proteins were not delivered properly to the podocyte cell membrane.
checks.evidence_quote: We found that mutant KIRREL1 proteins failed to localize to the podocyte cell membrane, indicating defective trafficking and impaired podocytes function.
checks.explanation: The paper reports reduced membrane localization and a trafficking defect.

checks.claim: In functional studies by Solanki et al. (2019), the KIRREL1 mutations impaired the interaction of KIRREL1 with other slit diaphragm components, such as nephrin.
checks.explanation: The paper did not test interaction between KIRREL1 and nephrin. It reports only that 'the KIRREL1 mutations did not affect membrane localization of NPHS1', which gives no evidence of impaired interaction.

paragraphs.text: Donoviel et al. (2001) found that mice lacking Neph1 (Kirrel1) developed proteinuria, had podocyte foot process effacement and died early in life. This showed that Neph1 is needed for the glomerular filtration barrier to work normally.

checks.claim: Donoviel et al. (2001) found that mice lacking Neph1 (Kirrel1) developed proteinuria.
checks.evidence_quote: Neph1-deficient mice develop nephrotic syndrome at birth
checks.explanation: The abstract says the mice develop nephrotic syndrome, which includes proteinuria, but it does not mention proteinuria in these mice or name Donoviel et al. (2001).

checks.claim: Donoviel et al. (2001) found that mice lacking Neph1 (Kirrel1) had podocyte foot process effacement.
checks.evidence_quote: Deletion of Kirrel in a mouse model results in podocyte foot processes effacement phenotype causing loss of glomerular filtration function.
checks.explanation: The paper states the finding but does not attribute it to Donoviel et al. (2001).

checks.claim: Donoviel et al. (2001) found that mice lacking Neph1 (Kirrel1) died early in life.
checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 2 cited papers. The abstract does not mention early death of Neph1-deficient mice. Only the abstract was supplied.

checks.claim: The findings of Donoviel et al. (2001) in Neph1-deficient mice showed that Neph1 is needed for the glomerular filtration barrier to work normally.
checks.evidence_quote: Neph1-deficient mice develop nephrotic syndrome at birth, indicating the importance of this protein in the development of a normal glomerular filtration barrier.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this conclusion about the knockout mice, although it does not name Donoviel et al.

clinical_synopsis.feature: Progression to end-stage renal disease in some patients

references.label: Solanki et al. (2019)
references.citation: Solanki AK, Widmeier E, Arif E, Sharma S, Daga A, Srivastava P, Kwon SH, Hugo H, Nakayama M, Mann N, and others. Mutations in KIRREL1, a slit diaphragm component, cause steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome. Kidney Int 96: 883-889, 2019. [PubMed: 31472902]
